tagline: An old railroad grade follows rapids through the Deschutes canyon
intro: The Lower Deschutes River Back Country Byway follows the river’s east bank for 32 miles. BLM presents close views of rapids and steep canyon country as the drive’s defining features. Twelve miles between Maupin and Highway 216 near Sherars Falls are paved; the remaining miles are graded gravel suitable for passenger vehicles. Developed recreation sites provide river access throughout the year, with boat launches, day-use areas and campgrounds distributed along the route.

Much of the road occupies a former railbed. E. H. Harriman and James J. Hill competed to build routes up the canyon, linking Columbia River mainlines with Central Oregon markets. Harriman’s company built a house at Maupin for the local track-maintenance foreman. Most of its canyon tracks were abandoned in 1936; the road in front of the house now uses the railroad grade. The station’s depot and maintenance-crew bunkhouse were demolished by 1968, leaving the foreman’s house beside the road.

Travel south from the northern terminus at Macks Canyon Campground toward Sherars Falls and the paved connection near Highway 216. Continue to Maupin, where U.S. 197 crosses the Deschutes, then pass the restored foreman’s house just south of town. The southern stretch ends at Locked Gate Day Use Area.

moments.title: Sherars Falls
moments.text: Sherars Falls is the Deschutes River’s last waterfall before the Columbia, a drop of about 15 feet near Sherar’s Bridge north of Maupin. Tribal fishers use dip nets here to catch salmon and steelhead for subsistence, working from boulders and platforms built by tribal members. The falls take their name from Joseph Sherar, a nineteenth-century wagon-road builder. The crossing upstream was used by wagon trains continuing west to bypass The Dalles.

moments.title: Maupin
moments.text: A ferry crossing survives in Maupin’s sequence of names: Hunts Ferry, then Maupin Ferry, then Maupin. William H. Staats, the town’s founder, made the change to Maupin Ferry. Howard Maupin, the namesake, had a farm and ferry here in the late nineteenth century. U.S. 197 now crosses the Deschutes in town at one of the few crossings north of Madras. Fishing and rafting connect much of the local economy to the river.

moments.title: Section Foreman's House
moments.text: The house beside the road south of Maupin once housed the foreman responsible for maintaining this section of railroad. Harriman’s Des Chutes Railroad Company built it in 1910 using a Union Pacific standard plan. It belonged to a three-building country station created during the competition to connect Columbia River rail lines with Central Oregon markets. The station also had a depot and a maintenance-crew bunkhouse, both demolished by 1968. BLM acquired the house that year. Restored and open seasonally, it contains interpretive displays and river information; the road outside follows the old railroad grade.
